segments.title: A fictional nuclear-coercion plan undone by a failed detonator
segments.summary: During the shelf build, Dr. Clarke recalls an unnamed geopolitical thriller in which a covert nuclear operation against Japan fails because its remote-detonation system was never viable.
segments.body: Dr. Clarke briefly turns from carpentry to the plot of an unnamed geopolitical thriller, not an account of an actual Russia-Japan war. In the story, a deniable Russian mission uses a diesel submarine and commandos to place nuclear weapons in a Japanese harbor that he recalls as Tokyo Bay. The scheme is meant to coerce Japan through a remotely controlled threat. It collapses when the submarine crew discovers that the poorly made control box provides no real way to detonate the warheads at a distance, leaving the weapons open to disarmament. The anecdote makes a useful strategic point: covert coercion depends not only on access and secrecy, but also on credible command-and-control and reliable equipment.

evidence.note: Dr. Clarke describes an unnamed book's fictional war between Russia and Japan, a deniable Russian operation, a diesel submarine, commandos, and nuclear weapons.
He explains that a poorly made box exposed the absence of a working remote detonator, allowing the submarine crew to disarm the weapons.
He closes by connecting the plot's technical failure to a joke about the quality of a villain's carpenters.
